Commercial Roof Coatings: A Complete Owner's Reference

Silicone, acrylic, and urethane roof coatings — what restoration coatings actually do, when they're the right economic move, when they fail, and how to buy them well.

Editorially reviewed Editorial review: Hila Atlan, Founder & Editor-in-Chief Updated July 21, 2026 4 sources cited 3 min read Editorial standards · Report an error

Key takeaways

  • A coating is not a new roof: it's UV and weathering protection for a roof that is still fundamentally sound.
  • The candidacy test is moisture: coating over a wet roof seals the problem in. Survey first, always.
  • Silicone leads on ponding resistance; acrylic is the value option on sloped, draining roofs; urethane is the trade pick for traffic — but capability is product-specific, so verify the data sheet.
  • Coatings shift roofing from capital replacement to maintenance cycles — often with tax treatment implications worth a CPA conversation.

What a roof coating is

A fluid-applied elastomeric layer — typically silicone, acrylic, or urethane — installed over an existing membrane, metal, or BUR/mod-bit roof after cleaning, repairs, and priming. It restores weathering surface, adds reflectivity, and defers tear-off. It does not add plies, fix wet insulation, or forgive a failing substrate.

The three chemistries

SiliconeAcrylicUrethane
Ponding waterStrongPoor (water-based; ponding accelerates degradation)Good
UV durabilityExcellentGoodGood
CostMid-highLowHigh
Traffic/abrasionFair (slick when wet)FairStrong
Typical roleFlat roofs, ponding-proneSloped metal, draining roofsHigh-traffic zones, base coats

These are the standard trade characterizations, drawn from manufacturer literature and trade practice rather than independent testing — and RCMA itself cautions that ponding capability is product-specific, not a chemistry-wide guarantee. Verify the specific product’s data sheet, not the category’s reputation. Hybrid systems (urethane base + silicone top) are common on demanding roofs.

When a coating is the right call

  • Membrane aged but dry (verified by moisture survey) and well-adhered.
  • Leak history limited to details, not field saturation.
  • Owner wants roughly another decade of service without tear-off disruption (RCMA’s published figure is “10 years or more” per properly applied cycle) or wants to phase capital.
  • Energy math favors reflectivity — see White vs. Black.

When it is the wrong call

  • Wet insulation beyond small, replaceable areas. There is no single industry cut-off for how much saturation disqualifies a roof — thresholds vary by manufacturer and surveyor, so get the number that governs your warranty in writing.
  • Poor adhesion substrate (aged PVC late in plasticizer loss, chalked or contaminated surfaces failing pull tests).
  • A roof at structural or attachment end-of-life — coatings don’t fix uplift.

Decision framework

  1. Moisture survey (infrared or capacitance). Wet areas are cut out and replaced, or the coating conversation ends.
  2. Adhesion pull tests on the actual roof, not brochure claims.
  3. Warranty reality check: coating warranties vary wildly in what counts as a leak and what maintenance they require — read exclusions before signing, and see the full comparison for the economics.
  4. Spec the system, not the bucket: mils of dry film thickness, reinforcement at details, and repair scope determine outcomes; the brand name doesn’t.

Common failure modes

  • Coating over moisture — blistering and adhesion loss (buyer’s failure, not the product’s).
  • Under-application — thin mils age out early; require wet/dry mil logs.
  • Detail shortcuts — un-reinforced seams and penetrations telegraph through.
  • Wrong chemistry for the exposure — acrylic in ponding zones being the classic.

Cost considerations

Coatings typically price well below replacement, varying with repair scope and system — a trade estimate quoted in coating-industry press puts silicone restoration at roughly half the installed cost of tear-off, but that is a manufacturer executive’s figure, not independent benchmarking, and repair scope can move it substantially. Coatings may also qualify as maintenance expense rather than capital improvement in some situations (tax treatment is fact-specific — consult your CPA), and many can be recoated at end of cycle, compounding the deferral.

Maintenance guidance

Annual inspection and cleaning; recoat on the cycle the manufacturer specifies for the system; maintain drainage; document everything for warranty continuity.

Frequently asked questions

Do coatings stop leaks? Coatings waterproof surfaces; they don’t repair failed systems. Leaks are fixed first, then the coating protects the fix.

How long does a coated roof last? The honest answer is a cycle, not a lifespan: RCMA’s published figure is “10 years or more” for a properly applied coating, renewable by recoat if the substrate stays sound. Manufacturers sell longer terms tied to heavier applied thickness — treat those as warranty terms, not lifespan promises.

Is a coating warranty as good as a new-roof warranty? Sometimes, and sometimes it’s marketing. Compare leak-coverage terms, exclusions (ponding, traffic), and maintenance requirements line by line.

Sources

  1. ASTM D6083/D6083M — Standard Specification for Liquid-Applied Acrylic Coating Used in Roofing — ASTM InternationalConfirms liquid-applied water-based acrylic elastomeric roof coating as a defined material class and sets its property requirements (solids, viscosity, tensile, elongation, weathering, adhesion). Verified against the current ASTM catalogue entry (D6083/D6083M-24). It standardises the acrylic material only — it does not cover silicone or urethane coatings, application, or in-service coating life.
  2. Roof Coating FAQs — Roof Coatings Manufacturers Association (industry association)Coating chemistries (acrylics, urethanes, silicones, others); that coatings extend roof life and reduce heat transfer; that a properly applied coating's protection 'can be extended up to 10 years or more' and is renewable by recoat; that some — not all — coatings are designed to withstand ponding, so capability is product-specific; and that existing leaks, wet insulation, or damaged deck call for a contractor before coating. RCMA is the coating manufacturers' trade association — promotional interest, no independent field data.
  3. Coatings Tech Note 8 — Acrylic Roof Coatings for Building Owners (August 2024) — Roof Coatings Manufacturers Association (industry association)That acrylic coatings are water-based, that 'ponding water could accelerate their degradation and negatively impact the longevity,' and that cold-weather application is limited. Manufacturer-association guidance, not independent research; covers acrylics only.
  4. Silicone Roof Coatings — WATERPROOF! Magazine (trade press, April 2018)Silicone's ponding-water resistance relative to acrylics, its UV stability, and its recoatability (silicone adheres to itself). Also the source of the 'roughly half the installed cost of tear-off' trade estimate — a manufacturer executive's figure quoted in trade press, not independent cost benchmarking. Article quotes coating-industry executives throughout; treat performance claims directionally.
